entities.name: Byzantine Empire under the Justinian dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Byzantine Empire under the Justinian dynasty (518-602 CE) achieved the last great attempt to restore the Roman Empire in the West, with Justinian I (r. 527-565 CE) reconquering North Africa (533), Italy (535-554), and southern Spain (552), briefly unifying the Mediterranean under Roman rule for the first time since 395 CE. The 'Justinianic Age' also produced the Corpus Juris Civilis (529-534 CE) — the systematic codification of Roman law that became the foundation of civil law systems governing two-thirds of the modern world.

Justinian I is history's paradigmatic 'sleepless emperor': working through the night, managing every detail of the vast empire, issuing 500+ novel laws, commissioning the rebuilding of the Hagia Sophia (532-537 CE, the world's greatest building for a millennium), launching simultaneous campaigns in Persia, Africa, Italy, and the Danube frontier, and surviving the 532 Nika Riots (in which 30,000 were killed and Constantinople nearly destroyed) only because his wife Empress Theodora refused to flee ('purple makes a fine burial shroud'). General Belisarius executed these military campaigns with minimal resources.

The Justinianic Plague (541-549 CE) — possibly history's first pandemic of bubonic plague — killed an estimated 25-50 million people (25-50% of the population), devastated the reconquest effort, and contributed to the eventual collapse of Justinian's expensive ambitions. His successors lost Italy to the Lombards (568) and could not maintain his Mediterranean empire. The dynasty ended with Emperor Maurice's 602 murder by the soldier Phocas — triggering Heraclius's coup and the next dynasty.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Justinian dynasty — producing the Corpus Juris Civilis (foundation of civil law governing 60% of the world), Hagia Sophia (world's greatest building for a millennium), and the last attempt to restore Roman Empire — shaped global legal civilization and produced two of history's most consequential intellectual and architectural monuments.
